newsitem.title: USA: Profitable year expected for Iowa hog farmers.
newsitem.headline: Profitable year expected for Iowa hog farmers.

text.p: Iowa pork producers attending their annual Pork Congress here were told that they could expect 1997 profits to rise as production costs ease.
"We are going to have a profitable year in 1997 for pork producers," John Lawrence, Iowa State University livestock extension economist, told a pork price forecasting seminar.

Lawrence forecast hog prices to average in the mid-$50 per cwt in the Iowa-Southern Minnesota area with average cost of production in the low $40 per cwt range. This would equate to a $20 to $25 per head or more profit for producers in 1997.

Iowa pork producers on average showed a profit in 1996 but some showed a loss of nearly $8 per head while others posted profits as high as $18 per head, he said. High live hog prices generally offset production costs. Producers who raised their own corn to feed did very well, Lawrence said.
Expected lower feed costs this year should raise profits and may stimulate an expansion in hog production, he said.

Lawrence said Iowa producers have incentive to expand with profits seen higher and outside influences easing, especially regarding enviromental issues with a new law, House File 519, setting legal and pollution standards for state producers.
HF 519 is more likely to benefit larger operations that can afford to build bigger and better waste storage and handling systems with full-time managers, Lawrence said.
"I think some of these restrictions are actually going to favor some of the larger producers," he said.

Iowa has room for expansion based on current production levels compared to packer capacity. Iowa packers process about 31 to 32 million hogs a year, more than one-third of the hogs slaughtered in the United States. But Iowa farmers only farrow around 17 million hogs a year. About 4-5 million feeder pigs are imported annually to be finished in Iowa, he added.

Asked about the dwindling number of pork producers in Iowa and across the U.S., Lawrence said the reductions came in the ranks of small operations. In the past 10 years, 82 percent of hog farms that closed down had fewer than 100 head of hogs. The other 18 percent had between 100 and 500 head, he said.
"If you take those farms that had at least 500 (head) in 1986, marketing 1,000 head or more, we actually have more of those farms today than we did a decade ago," Lawrence said.
"The commercial-size family operation is going quiet well and we have more of them," he said.

LeRoy Stoltenberg, outgoing Iowa Pork Producers Association president, said those producers showing a faster rate of expansion in Iowa are usually family operations that have a father and his sons or a family of brothers.
